scenario: AITA for 'stealing' my Dad's business idea and making a success of it? | Title says it all really. I (26M) technically ''stole'' my dad's business idea. When I first heard it from him, it was so simple yet so...genius. I can't say exactly what it is here, but it was genius. The thing is, me and my dad (55M) are complete opposites. He's the more introverted and quiet type. He's always been *very* intelligent, but he's lacked the ability to *get things done.* I've been told I'm more like my grandad (75M, my dad's dad). Physically, I look more like my grandad, but personality wise, I guess I'm a bit more impulsive and hot headed and not as intelligent as my dad, but I get things done. Perhaps I'm more ''traditional masculine'' than my dad. Its like I should be in the older generation, and he should be from the newer one. When I heard my Dad's business idea, I was amazed, but I didn't truly believe my Dad could pull it off. He doesn't get things done. He's always been full of great ideas, but ideas not put to use are useless. So I took the idea and ran with it. I got IP rights and started the business with it 2 years ago. Since then, its been a massive success. Not millions or anything, but into the six figures and the potential to make millions is there perhaps in the next half decade if things keep going well. My dad was very upset when I did this, but didn't say much. I could tell by his facial expressions. My mom (55F) said I've done her proud and done the right thing. Well I confronted my dad yesterday to ask him how he feels and he said I'm a ''fucking asshole''. He said he felt betrayed by me and nearly started crying. I told him straight, ''You've always been a man of ideas, but I'm a man of action''. Then my sister (28F) walks in and starts saying shit to me, defending my dad. Both my mom and granddad have taken my side. I even offered my dad 20% of all profits, but he rejected and told me to get out. I understand why he's upset, but I think he's being unreasonable here. AITA?

First, from my point of view: I saw a great idea that my dad wasn't acting on, so I took the initiative to make it successful. I secured IP rights, started the business, and it's been a huge success. I even offered him a share of the profits, which shows I'm willing to compensate him for his idea. From my dad's perspective: He came up with the idea, which he probably felt was his. When I took it without his consent and started a business, he felt betrayed. He might feel that I stole his idea and didn't give him proper credit or compensation, even though I offered him a share later. My mom and granddad support me, which suggests they see my actions as reasonable, especially since I've made the business successful. My sister, however, is defending my dad, which indicates she might see my actions as disrespectful or unfair. So, is AITA? To determine that, I need to assess whether my actions were reasonable or if I'm being the asshole here. First, did I steal the idea? Well, I didn't take it without any consideration. I thought it was genius and doubted my dad's ability to execute it. But did I have the right to take it without his consent? That's a gray area. Ideas are intangible, and while I can respect his ownership of the idea, I also took action to make it successful. Second, did I offer him a fair share? I offered him 20% of the profits, which is significant. However, he rejected it, which might indicate he feels the issue is more about recognition and betrayal than just financial compensation. Third, how did I handle the confrontation? I told him I'm a man of action, which might have come off as dismissive of his feelings. Maybe I could have approached the conversation more empathetically. Fourth, considering the family dynamics: My mom and granddad support me, but my sister is on my dad's side. This could create tension within the family, which is important to consider. So, in summary, while I took initiative and made the business successful, I might have overlooked the emotional and relational aspects of taking my dad's idea without his consent.
